title: Breakthrough
summary: Giving up one or two pawns to create a passed pawn, after counting whether the enemy king gets there in time.
part.classic.title: The classic breakthrough
part.classic.summary: Three pawns against three, kings far away: the middle pawn is sacrificed, then its neighbour deflects the guard, and the third one queens.
part.count.title: Count before you sacrifice
part.count.summary: A pawn given is a pawn gone. Before the first one, check whether the enemy king catches the new passer; if it does, bring your own king, as Capablanca should have.
part.order.title: Fix before you break
part.order.summary: Two advances that look alike: the one that makes contact first lets the new pawn be born a square further up.
part.side.title: Far from the king
part.side.summary: The passed pawn has to be born on the side where the enemy king isn't; and a king tied to one passer can't look after another.
part.pushPast.title: Don't take: pass
part.pushPast.summary: Pawns in contact: capturing is the natural move and often loses. The pawn that gets through is the one that does not capture, as in Capablanca against Edward Lasker.
part.kingFirst.title: King first, then the breakthrough
part.kingFirst.summary: If the opponent has a passed pawn too, the race of the two queens is a draw: the king steps in front of it before you break.
part.defense.title: The defence
part.defense.summary: The defender to move pushes a pawn into contact before the breakthrough; with the king close, the king goes after the pawns.
part.finish.title: Summary
part.finish.summary: Three rules for your games, the defence as the mirror image, the blow once more and the practical challenge.
step.t_classic: White to move. Three pawns against three, face to face, and both kings far away. No pawn is passed, and the black king can't help. Can White get a pawn to the eighth rank?
step.t_classic.hint1: One pawn alone can't get past three. But if you give away one or two pawns, the black pawns must capture and step out of the way; and if they don't capture, the pawn that advanced captures and queens.
step.t_classic.hint2: Which pawn, when it advances, threatens two black pawns at the same time?
step.classicWhy: b6! It threatens bxa7 and bxc7, with a queen right after, so Black has to capture. Whether Black takes with the a-pawn or the c-pawn, one file is left unguarded in front of a pawn of mine, and the other pawn sacrifices itself to deflect whoever still guards that file. Watch the capture with the a-pawn first.
step.d_classic: Black took with the a-pawn. The a-file is free in front of my a5-pawn; only the b7-pawn still guards a6. Watch the second sacrifice.
step.d_classic.m1: c6! Another pawn given away, on purpose. It threatens cxb7 and, if Black doesn't take, it reaches c8.
step.d_classic.m2: Black takes. The b7-pawn has left the b-file, and it was the one guarding a6.
step.d_classic.m3: a6. No black pawn can touch this pawn. Two moves to the queen.
step.d_classic.m4: The black king runs. To catch the pawn, it would have to reach b7 before the promotion.
step.d_classic.m5: a7. One square from the queen. The black king would have to be on b7 right now, and it is on f7: the queen comes next move. Notice the black pawns on b6 and c6, a long way from the first rank.
step.otherCapture: And if Black takes with the c-pawn? It's the mirror image. Now the c-file has no black pawn in front of my c5-pawn, and only the b7-pawn guards c6. The second sacrifice is a6!, to deflect that pawn. After the first sacrifice, look at which file became free: that file's pawn is the one that will get through.
step.classicMove: Your turn. Black took with the c-pawn. White to move and win.
step.classicMove.hint: The c-file is free in front of your c5-pawn. Who guards c6? Deflect that pawn.
step.classicMove.done: That's it. a6 deflected the b7-pawn, and the c-pawn went straight through. Only that path won.
step.t_count: Same idea, but now the black king is on e8, closer. White has already played b6 and Black took with the a-pawn. Does the breakthrough still work? Count before you play.
step.t_count.hint1: Play the breakthrough in your head to the end: c6, bxc6, a6. Now it's Black's move. Where must the king get to in order to stop the a6-pawn?
step.t_count.hint2: The a6-pawn queens in two moves. The black king has to reach b7 first. Count the king moves from e8, remembering that c7 is taken by a black pawn.
step.square: It's a count of moves. After c6, bxc6 and a6, the pawn is two squares from queening, and Black is to move. The king on e8 needs three moves to reach b7: d8, c8, b7. The pawn needs two. The king is too late, and the breakthrough works. One move less, and it would fail.
step.tooClose: Another structure: three pawns against two, and the black king on d8, right on top of the pawns. Here any breakthrough, b6, c6 or d6, only draws: the new pawn is born next to the king, and the king catches it. But with an extra pawn I don't need to break. The plan is to bring the king, Kf2, Ke3, Kd4, and only advance the pawns with the king alongside. When the count says the enemy king gets there, keep the breakthrough for later and bring your own king.
step.capaCount: Masters get this count wrong too. This is the ending of Capablanca against Edward Lasker, a friendly game in London, 1913. Capablanca played 39.f5?, and after 39...gxf5 40.h5 the black king could come back with 40...Ke6 and hold: the breakthrough had come too early. The right preparation was 39.a3!, keeping a4 in reserve for the moment the black king ran out of good squares; only then f5 and h5. Count before you break; if the count doesn't work, improve the position first.
step.countMove: Back to the king on e8. White to move and win. Make the breakthrough and take the pawn to the seventh rank.
step.countMove.hint: You've already counted: the king on e8 arrives late. Deflect the b7-pawn and run with the a-pawn.
step.countMove.done: That's it. The black king went to d7, but the pawn is already on a7 and queens next move.
step.t_order: White to move. Two pawns against one on the queenside, b4 and c4 against b6, and the black king far away on g5, with its g6-pawn. The two advances, b5 and c5, look alike. Only one wins. Which, and why?
step.t_order.hint1: After the breakthrough, Black is left with a passed pawn too. Count both races to the last rank.
step.t_order.hint2: One of the advances lets your new pawn be born a square closer to b8.
step.orderWhy: b5! Fix first: the b6-pawn is pinned down, with my b5-pawn in contact with it. Now c5 comes with force: bxc5 b6, and the passed pawn is already born on b6, two moves from the queen. The black c5-pawn needs three moves to reach c2 and one more to queen. Mine gets there first, and the new queen stops the c-pawn.
step.orderWrong: In the wrong order, c5? bxc5 b5, the passed pawn is born on b5, not b6: one move behind. Black plays c4, and the two races finish together, b6 c3 b7 c2 b8=Q c1=Q, queen against queen, a draw. One square of difference, and the pawn you fixed first is the one that wins it.
step.orderMove: Your turn, from the same position. White to move and win. Fix first, then break.
step.orderMove.hint: Which advance lets your new pawn be born a square further up? Make contact with the b6-pawn before you give up the c-pawn.
step.orderMove.done: That's it. b5 fixed the b6-pawn, c5 deflected it, and the passed pawn was already born on b6: it queens before Black's c-pawn.
step.t_side: White to move. Different pawns: White on c5 and e5, Black on d7, e7 and d6. The black king is on h8. There's a breakthrough here. With which pawn?
step.t_side.hint1: Try both advances, c6 and e6. After each one, a black pawn captures. Which white pawn is left with a free file?
step.t_side.hint2: One of the advances leaves the e5-pawn still blocked by the e7-pawn. The other frees a pawn on a file far from the black king.
step.sideWhy: e6! It threatens exd7 and queening. If the d7-pawn takes, the c5-pawn has nobody in front or beside it: c6, c7, c8. And the black king on h8 is on the other side of the board. c6? is no use: the e5-pawn would still be blocked by the e7-pawn. That's what changes from the classic: here there is no middle pawn to sacrifice, and the right advance is the one that frees a pawn on a file far from the king.
step.d_side: Now the mirror image: black pawns on c7, d7 and d6, and the black king on a8, close to the c-file. e6 would not win here: the c-pawn would be born next to the king. The breakthrough is on the other side.
step.d_side.m1: c6! It threatens cxd7 and queening on d8: Black has to capture.
step.d_side.m2: Black takes, and the e7-pawn has left the e-file: it is free in front of my pawn.
step.d_side.m3: e6. Nobody can touch this pawn, and the black king is at the far end.
step.d_side.m4: The black king comes, but from b7 it can't reach d7 or e8 in time.
step.d_side.m5: e7. One square from the queen; the king would have to be on d7 or e8 right now, and it is on b7. The queen comes next move.
step.twoPassers: One step further. Here I already have a passed pawn, on a6, and the black king on a8 is tied to it: if the king walks away, a7 and a8. But a single king can't watch two passed pawns on different wings. My pawns on e4 and f4 against the one on f6 hide the breakthrough that creates the second passer, far from the king. Watch.
step.d_twoPassers: The black king can't leave the a6-pawn. So I break far away from it.
step.d_twoPassers.m1: e5! I give the e-pawn to open the f-file: if the f6-pawn takes, the f4-pawn is free.
step.d_twoPassers.m2: Black takes. The f6-pawn has left the f-file.
step.d_twoPassers.m3: f5. The second passed pawn is born, and the black king is on the other side, tied to the a6-pawn.
step.d_twoPassers.m4: The black king leaves the corner, but can't move away from the a-pawn: if it heads for the centre, a7 and a queen.
step.d_twoPassers.m5: f6. Two passed pawns on different wings against a single king: it can't reach both. The f-pawn queens.
step.sideMove: Back to the king on h8. White to move and win.
step.sideMove.hint: Advance the pawn that forces the d7-pawn to capture and frees the pawn on the file far from the king.
step.sideMove.done: That's it. e6 pulled the d7-pawn out of the way, and the c-pawn went alone to c7. The black king never came close.
step.t_push: Back to Capablanca against Edward Lasker, London, 1913, two moves later. Capablanca broke through with 39.f5 and 40.h5, and Lasker has just played 40...Ke5. White to move. Taking on g6, with 41.g6 hxg6 42.h6, is the natural move and clears the way for the h-pawn. Is it right?
step.t_push.hint1: Play g6 in your head to the end: hxg6, h6, and now the black king goes to f6. Does it reach the h-pawn?
step.t_push.hint2: What if no pawn captured right now? One of yours can walk past the black pawn, and then g6 comes with more force.
step.pushWhy: 41.h6!! Capablanca did not capture. The black king can't even go back to f6, because the g5-pawn covers that square, and 42.g6 comes next move whatever Black does: if 42...hxg6, 43.h7 and a queen; if not, 43.gxh7 and a queen. Lasker resigned. 41.g6? first was the mistake: 41...hxg6 42.h6 Kf6, the king reaches the h-pawn, and Black would win with the f- and d-pawns. The pawn that gets through is the one that does not capture.
step.d_push: The same idea in a clean position: pawns on a6 and b5 against a7 and b7, the black king on d7. Taking on b7 is natural and only draws: axb7 Kc7, and the king picks up the pawn. Watch the move that passes.
step.d_push.m1: b6! I don't take on b7: I make contact. If axb6, a7 and the pawn queens; if bxa6, bxa7 and it queens the other way.
step.d_push.m3: a7. The a6-pawn walked past the b7-pawn without capturing: the b7-pawn only covers a6 and c6, and a7 was free.
step.d_push.m4: The black king runs, but the pawn is already on a7: it arrives one move too late.
step.d_push.m5: Queen. Taking on b7 would have let the king catch the pawn; the winning move was the one that walked past.
step.pushMove: Your turn. Pawns on c5 and d6 against c7 and d7, the black king on a7. Taking on c7 is natural. White to move and win.
step.pushMove.hint: After dxc7, the king goes to b7 and picks up the pawn. These are the two central files, not the edge: which pawn makes contact without capturing, and which one walks past?
step.pushMove.done: That's it. c6 made contact without capturing; Black took on c6, the d-file opened and the d6 pawn walked past and queens, far from the king. With Black to move, Black would be the one winning; and taking on c7 only drew.
step.t_kingFirst: White to move. The f5 breakthrough is ready: f5, gxf5, h5 and the h-pawn runs. But Black has the passed c6-pawn, and your king is on a1, in the corner. Break now?
step.t_kingFirst.hint1: After f5 gxf5 h5, Black is left with a passed pawn too: the one that captured on f5. Count both races.
step.t_kingFirst.hint2: What stops an enemy passed pawn is not a pawn of yours: it's your king. Where does it need to be before the breakthrough?
step.kingFirstWhy: f5? gxf5 h5, and the black f-pawn runs: f4, h6, f3, h7, f2, h8=Q, f1=Q. The two queens are born together, and the c6-pawn is still on the board: a draw. The breakthrough creates a passed pawn for each side, and your king on a1 reaches neither the f-pawn nor the c-pawn. King first, Kb2! It heads for the centre, steps into the square of both black pawns, and the breakthrough waits.
step.kingFirstPath: The path is Kb2, Kc2 and Kd1. Black runs with the c-pawn, c5 and c4, but from d1 the king stops that pawn and still reaches the f-pawn when it is born. Mind the square: Kd2? already only draws. Black answers Kc5 and, in the race f5 gxf5 h5 f4 h6 f3 h7, plays c3 with check at just the right moment: my king loses the tempo and both queens are born together. From d1, c3 is not check. With the king on d1, f5 wins: gxf5 h5, and the h-pawn queens on its own, because the black king is on the other wing.
step.kingFirstMove: Your turn. Bring the king first and only then break. White to move and win.
step.kingFirstMove.hint: The king goes in front of the c-pawn, along the squares where it doesn't get checked; the f5 breakthrough only after the king reaches d1.
step.kingFirstMove.done: That's it. King on d1, both black pawns watched, and only then f5 and h5: now it's a race of one pawn only.
step.t_defense: Now you defend. White pawns on f5, g5 and h5 against yours on f7, g7 and h7, and your king on g3, far from the eighth rank. If it were White's move, g6! would be the b6 of the first part, and a pawn would get through. But it's your move. How do you take the breakthrough away?
step.t_defense.hint1: Waiting with the king doesn't help: g6 comes. Look for a pawn move that takes the middle sacrifice away from White.
step.t_defense.hint2: One of your three pawns can advance and touch the white pawns. Only one of them holds.
step.defenseWhy: ...g6! The defender pushes the middle pawn into contact before the attacker does. Now, if White captures, hxg6 or fxg6, the pawns get exchanged and no white pawn gets through; and my pawn on g6 means White's g6 can no longer happen. The other advances, ...f6 and ...h6, hand over the breakthrough through the neighbouring pawn: only ...g6 holds.
step.defenseMove: Black played ...g6, and White took with the h-pawn. Black to move and draw. Which pawn do you recapture with?
step.defenseMove.hint: Recapture with the pawn on the same side the white pawn came from. That way the other white pawn still has a black pawn in front of it.
step.defenseMove.done: That's it. After fxg6 and fxg6, one pawn each is left, blocked: a draw. Had you taken with the f-pawn, f6! would have given White a passed pawn.
step.defenseKing: With the king close, the defence gains a second resource. Here it is three white pawns against two, a5, b5 and c5 against a7 and b7, and your king on d7. There is no middle pawn to push into contact; what holds is ...a6!, making contact from the side. If bxa6, bxa6, and the a-pawns block each other while your king looks after the c-pawn. If White advances b6, your king goes after the pawns, Kc6!, and the c5-pawn falls. With the king close, the rule is: make contact before the breakthrough and take the king in front of whatever pawn is left.
step.defenseKingMove: Black to move and draw. Make contact first, then bring the king.
step.defenseKingMove.hint: The pawn that makes contact is the outside one, there is no middle pawn. Then, if White advances, the king attacks the pawns.
step.defenseKingMove.done: That's it. ...a6 took the breakthrough away, and the king went to collect the c5-pawn. No passed pawn, no win.
step.recap: Three rules for your games. First: three against three, face to face, the middle pawn is sacrificed first; then its neighbour deflects the guard of the file that became free. Second: before you give up the pawn, count. If the enemy king catches the new pawn, bring your king first or don't break; if the opponent has a passed pawn too, your king steps in front of it before the breakthrough. Third: when the pawns are in contact, fix or pass instead of capturing: the pawn that gets through is the one that does not capture.
step.recapDefense: And the defence is the mirror image. The defender to move pushes a pawn into contact before the breakthrough: the middle one, when there is one; the outside one, when there isn't. Recapture with the pawn on the same side and take the king in front of whatever pawn is left.
step.recapMove: The blow once more, before the game. Black took with the a-pawn. White to move and win.
step.recapMove.hint: The a5-pawn has a free file; only the b7-pawn guards a6.
step.recapMove.done: That's it. c6 deflected the b7-pawn, and the a5-pawn got through.
step.playIntro: Now the practical challenge. Black has already taken with the a-pawn, and the black king is on f1, far away. Only one move wins. Count, and play on until you have a queen.
step.finish: White to move and win. Have a good game.
ex.e01: White to move and win. Two pawns against one, and the black king on d8.
ex.e01.hint: The a6-pawn is two squares from queening, but the a7-pawn is in the way. Get it out of the way.
ex.e01.solution: b6! If axb6, a7, and the king on d8 doesn't reach b7 in time. If Black doesn't take, for example with Kc8, bxa7 and the pawn queens. White's king moves only draw.
ex.e08: White to move and win. Three pawns against two, but the black king is on c8, right next to the pawns.
ex.e08.hint: Count before you sacrifice: after a breakthrough, does the black king catch the new pawn? If it does, look for another plan.
ex.e08.solution: Here the breakthrough only draws: the king on c8 catches the new pawn. With an extra pawn, the plan is to bring the king. Any king move, such as Kf2, wins; a6, b6 or c6 right now throw the win away.
ex.e10: Black to move and draw. Three white pawns against two, and the black king on d7. What do you do before White plays b6?
ex.e10.hint: Push a pawn into contact with the white pawns to take the breakthrough away, and let the king handle the rest.
ex.e10.solution: ...a6! After bxa6, the king goes to c8 and, after c6, to b8, in front of the a-pawn. The c7-pawn blocks the c6-pawn. Only ...a6 draws, and after that only Kc8 and Kb8 hold.
ex.e11: White to move and win. Two pawns against one: b4 and c4 against b6, with the black king on g5 and yours on h1. In what order do the pawns advance?
ex.e11.hint: The two advances look alike, but one of them leaves the new pawn a square closer to b8. And remember that, after the breakthrough, Black is left with a passed pawn too.
ex.e11.solution: b5! Fix first: after Kf4, c5! bxc5 and b6, the passed pawn is already on b6 and queens before Black's c-pawn. If c5 first, bxc5 b5 c4!, and both pawns queen together: a draw. Only b5 wins.
ex.e12: White to move and win. Your pawns on g5 and h6 are in contact with the black pawns on g7 and h7, kings on e5 and e7. Taking on g7 is the natural move. Count first.
ex.e12.hint: After hxg7, the black king goes to f7 and picks up the pawn. Look for a pawn move that leaves the black pawns without a good answer.
ex.e12.solution: g6! If gxh6, gxh7 and the pawn queens on h8; if hxg6, h7 and it queens the same way. But hxg7? loses: Kf7, the king picks up the g7-pawn and the a7-pawn decides later. Only g6 wins.
ex.e13: White to move and win. Your a6-pawn is passed, but the black king on c6 watches it; you still have c4 and e3 against c7 and d6. How do you create a second passed pawn?
ex.e13.hint: The black king can't look after two passed pawns on different wings. Which pawn sacrifices itself to open the way for the e-pawn?
ex.e13.solution: c5! After dxc5, e4!, and the e-pawn runs: if Kb6, e5; if Kxa6, e6 and e7, far from the king. If Black doesn't take on c5, cxd6 and White has two passed pawns. e4 at once allows Kb6, and the king gets back in time: a draw. a7 also only draws.
ex.e14: White to move and win. Kings on f8 and h8; your pawns on f2 and g4 against g6 and h5. Taking on h5 looks obvious. Is it?
ex.e14.hint: Let the h-pawn run: what matters is clearing the way for a pawn of yours that arrives with check. The f-pawn still has a part to play.
ex.e14.solution: g5! Not gxh5? gxh5, and Black's h-pawn gets there first. After h4, f4! h3, f5! gxf5 and g6: the g-pawn reaches g7 with check, queens on g8 with check and the new queen picks up the h-pawn. Each White move is the only one that wins.
ex.e15: White to move and win. Pawns on f4 and h4 against g6: the f5 breakthrough is ready. But Black has the c6-pawn, and your king is on a4. What comes first?
ex.e15.hint: If you break through now, the c-pawn queens together with yours. First the king steps into the c-pawn's path, and along the squares where it doesn't get checked.
ex.e15.solution: Kb3! If f5? gxf5 h5 f4 h6 f3 h7 f2 h8=Q f1=Q: a draw. After Kb3 c5, Kc2!, c4, Kd1! (on d2 the pawn would give check on c3 at the wrong moment) and only then, with the king in front of the pawn, f5! gxf5 h5, and the h-pawn queens. Five moves, each the only one that wins.
key.classic: Three pawns against three with the kings far away: White gives two pawns so the third can get through and promote. Only the right breakthrough wins.
key.afterAxb6: Black captured with the a-pawn: now White's c-pawn goes forward, and one of the two white pawns promotes.
key.afterCxb6: Black captured with the c-pawn: now White's a-pawn goes forward, and it gets through.
key.count: Count before you sacrifice: here the black king arrives one move too late, and the breakthrough still wins. With the king one square closer, it would fail.
key.capa: Capablanca against Edward Lasker, London, 1913: the white pawn advances without capturing anything, slips past the black pawn and can't be stopped.
key.order: Two pawns against one with the black king far away: first one white pawn fixes the black pawn, and only then comes the breakthrough.
key.side: The right breakthrough is the one that creates the passed pawn far from the black king, on the side it can't reach in time.
key.kingFirst: The breakthrough is ready, but it's too early: first the white king goes to hold the black pawn on the other side, and only then do the pawns advance.
key.wikiDefense: The same breakthrough on the kingside, now with Black to move: by pushing the middle pawn at the right moment, Black defuses the breakthrough and holds.
history: A breakthrough is when you give up one or two pawns on purpose to break through your opponent's pawn line and create a pawn that nobody can stop. It's one of the most beautiful weapons in pawn endings, and it comes up often: with the kings far away, a well-counted breakthrough decides the game on the spot. The secret is to count first: if the enemy king gets there in time to stop the new pawn, you've just lost material. All the great endgame manuals, such as Mark Dvoretsky's and Jesús de la Villa's, teach it. The master game in this lesson is a friendly played in London in 1913: the Cuban José Raúl Capablanca, who would later become world champion, got a pawn through without capturing anything, and Edward Lasker had to resign.
practice: Final training: White pawns on c5 and e5, Black pawns on d7, e7 and d6, and the black king on h8. Find the breakthrough and take the pawn all the way to a queen.
